implementation_notes: JavaScript absorbed the mute into syntax: since ES2019 a catch clause may omit the binding entirely (`try { call() } catch { /* documented */ }`), which is the language's way of saying the thrown value is intentionally unused - MDN spells the rule out as 'if you don't need the exception value, you can omit it along with the enclosing parentheses'. For rejected fire-and-forget promises the same intent is expressed by attaching an empty handler, `.catch(() => {})`, so the rejection is handled instead of reported as an unhandled rejection. In async/await code prefer the local try/catch over an orphaned promise, so the mute stays at the call it justifies.
pitfalls: Omitting the binding also omits the reason: `catch {}` cannot inspect or log the thrown value, so a later investigation has nothing to read - keep a console.debug when the failure has any diagnostic value.
`.catch(() => {})` on a promise hides rejections that would otherwise surface through the unhandledrejection event; attach it to the specific promise and never use it to silence a whole chain.

`catch {}` around an `await` inside a loop mutes per-iteration failures silently, which is a common source of 'nothing happened' production bugs; when the loop must continue, at least count the failures.
